title: What Computers Still Can't Do
subtitle: A Critique of Artificial Reason
pitch: A philosopher's famous attack on early AI: human intelligence rests on bodies, skills and context that rule based programs cannot capture.

chapters.g: Dreyfus reviews the bold predictions of 1950s and 1960s AI and why they kept failing.
Early AI assumed the brain works like a computer, the mind follows rules, all knowledge can be formalised, and the world is made of separate facts.
Much expertise is skill and intuition, not explicit rules.
Human understanding depends on having a body and being in a situation.
Looking back on twenty years, Dreyfus discusses why expert systems hit limits and what neural networks might change.

ideas: Symbolic AI rested on doubtful assumptions.
Expertise is often intuitive skill, not rules.
Context and the body matter for intelligence.
Neural networks might avoid some limits of rule based AI.

args.a: Rule based AI cannot reach human intelligence.
args.c: This held up well for symbolic AI. Deep learning learns from data rather than rules, which partly sidesteps his critique.
Large language models show surprising ability without bodies, though critics say they still lack real understanding.

questions: Which of the four assumptions do today's models still make?
Can intuition be learned from data?
Does an AI need a body to understand the world?
